title: Study Finds Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy in Vast Majority of Deceased NFL Players Studied
dek: A study of 235 former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 found 215 had chronic traumatic encephalopathy, placing prevalence between 24.5% and 97.7%, substantially higher than prior research. Researchers attribute cumulative head impacts across youth, high school, and college levels, not just professional play, as the driver.
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: Of 235 deceased former NFL players whose brains were donated to research, 215 were found to have chronic traumatic encephalopathy, a degenerative brain disease linked to repeated head impacts.
bottom_line: The study's findings extend the safety conversation beyond professional football to youth and college levels, where researchers say most cumulative head trauma occurs. What remains to be seen is whether leagues and youth programs at those levels adopt additional protective measures in response to the documented prevalence of CTE in players who reached the NFL.
body: A new study of deceased former NFL players has documented chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain disease linked to repeated head impacts, at rates substantially higher than previously reported in research literature.

According to reporting by BBC Sport, of 235 former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 and donated their brains to research, 215 were found to have CTE. The study, published in the British Medical Journal, calculates a conservative minimum prevalence of 24.5% among those who died in that six-year period, rising to a maximum of 97.7%.

Daniel Daneshvar, an associate professor at Harvard Medical School and lead author of the study, stated that former NFL players face elevated neurological risk compared with the general population. "In NFL players, specifically, there is about a four times higher rate of death from neurodegenerative disease than the general population," Daneshvar said, per BBC Sport. "These findings indicate that NFL players have a higher prevalence of CTE at death than has been previously shown in multiple community based studies."

The study found dementia to be common among the brain donors. Daneshvar attributed the disease burden not to NFL play alone but to cumulative impacts across multiple levels of football. "The bulk of the head impacts that these former NFL players experienced didn't occur at the NFL level," Daneshvar said, per BBC Sport. "They occurred at the collegiate level and at the high school level and in many cases the youth level. And all of those cumulative hits to the head added up to result in an increased risk."

Researchers have urged the NFL to take prevention measures to reduce repetitive head impacts across all levels of the sport, according to BBC Sport. The NFL has previously taken steps to address the issue: a 2011 Collective Bargaining Agreement limited the number of contact practices, and in 2016 the league agreed a $1 billion settlement with more than 5,000 former players following a class action lawsuit.

An NFL spokesperson responded to the study findings, per BBC Sport: "The NFL continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts. The NFL remains committed to ensuring that the NFL community has access to a robust and expanding set of resources to enhance their physical and mental well being. We encourage former players to utilise these resources to identify and seek treatment when they are concerned about their health."
